newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil soybean producers seen scratching for seeds.
newsitem.headline: Brazil soybean producers seen scratching for seeds.

text.p: Availability of certified quality soybean seeds this year is well below that of 1995 despite hopes of a larger overall crop, the executive director of the Brazilian Seed Producers' Association said.
"We just finished a survey at the end of September and there are 778,000 tonnes of certified seeds available this year," said Joao Henrique Hummel.
This is down from 840,000 tonnes in 1995 and 900,000 to one million tonnes in 1994, he added.
Brazilian analysts and producers are talking of a possible crop of around 26 million tonnes in 1996/97, up from a 1995/1996 harvest of 23.2 million tonnes.
In the 1995/96 crop planting, Brazil used 1.3 million tonnes of seeds, of which around 65 percent were certified.
"If people are talking about a 10 percent increase, then this year we need 1.4 million tonnes in total," Hummel said.
Given the shortage of certified seeds, farmers are likely to use a higher percentage of actual soybeans as seeds, leading to lower productivity, Hummel said.
"Usually farmers use 20 to 25 percent soybeans but this year it will be much higher," he added.
The expected seed shortage has led to an earlier than normal pick-up in demand for seeds, with prices on the rise.

In Rio Grande do Sul, traditionally the country's largest producing state, certified seeds are currently being sold for 22 to 30 reais ($21.57-29.41) a 50-kg bag against 14 reais ($13.73 a year ago, Hummel said.

In the key states of Parana and Rio Grande do Sul, the key planting period this year is likely to be November. The association hopes to have a clearer idea of actual seed sales by the beginning of next month, Hummel said.
